title: New Zealand cyclone wind — the 2023 season
summary: Peak 10 m gust per hex cell across Cyclones Hale and Gabrielle. New Zealand sees one or two landfalling cyclones a year. In 2023 it saw exactly two: Hale in January, which passed within 48 km of the coast, and Gabrielle in February, which caused the country's costliest weather disaster in decades. Both windows are analysed here.
body: The index is the highest 10 m gust each hex cell recorded during those events. Cells are 30 km across and clipped to the coastline — the payout question is about wind over land, so an ocean cell reading 200 km/h is a picture of the sea, not a claim.

This POC was originally scoped on a parametric windfield: cyclone best-track points driving a Holland vortex, the method used in production for Caribbean hurricane microinsurance. That does not survive contact with the New Zealand record. Gabrielle carries no intensity and no radius-of-maximum-wind at any of the 30 track points across its approach, and only three points in twenty-six years within 300 km of the coast carry both. The cause is institutional, not a data gap: the agencies that publish radius-of-maximum-wind have no responsibility for New Zealand, and the agency that does has never published the field. No alternative feed fixes that, so the hazard is reanalysis instead.

What the map is not: a priced product. The ladder shown is the Australian/NZ tropical cyclone category scale, which is correct as a legend and wrong as a payout trigger — 63 km/h is a genuine Category 1 boundary and also ordinary New Zealand weather, so tier 1 fires on most of the country most years. Calibrating it is a pricing decision.
caveats: ERA5 is a backtest and pricing input. Final ERA5 runs 2-3 months behind and ERA5T about 5 days, so a live product would trigger on station gusts, never on this.
Values are 28 km grid-cell averages. Exposed sites read higher: Auckland airport recorded 88.9 km/h during Gabrielle while exposed capes recorded 150-159 km/h.
Peak over the season's analysed cyclone events, not an annual maximum. A winter storm can out-blow a cyclone here.
No observed New Zealand cyclone loss series exists, so payout-versus-loss is recorded as not applicable rather than estimated.
